X moves the beam sideways. Y moves it up and down. Together, they draw.

A simulation, sparked by analog.

A drawing is two signals
moving together.

On an oscilloscope in X–Y mode, one voltage controls the beam’s horizontal position and another controls its vertical position. Changing both voltages over time traces a shape.

Explore the principle in Tektronix’s guide to X–Y display mode ↗.

X(t)Horizontal voltage
Y(t)Vertical voltage

Phosphor turns your text or image into a path, samples positions along it, and uses those positions as voltage signals. The two plots show one complete drawing cycle. Their moving cursor marks the same instant as the dot on the display.

Try the controls. Drawing speed changes how quickly the path repeats. X and Y gain stretch the drawing. Persistence lets earlier parts of the trace linger. Blanking hides the beam while it travels between separate strokes.

This is a visual simulation.

Voltages use a nominal ±5 V scale and playback is slowed so you can follow the beam. It does not output electrical signals or control hardware. CSV export contains the sampled X, Y, and blanking values for exploration.
